Substrate

Agentic OS (AOS)

Multi-agent orchestration framework · built in Claude Code

Every project on the dashboard runs on the same substrate: a framework I built, not a template I installed.

Every route through AOS ends one of two ways: an automatic execute for low-stakes, reversible work, or a hold for my explicit sign-off before anything that spends money, goes public, or can't be undone.

AOS manages agent state through a filesystem-as-system-bus model (plain files standing in for the RAM and disk tiers a traditional OS would use), so any agent's work is inspectable and resumable without a database or a running daemon. Cost and safety are structural, not aspirational: a tiered model-routing layer defaults every task to the cheapest, fastest model and escalates only on demonstrated need — what keeps a framework running dozens of agent tasks a day from burning through budget. A dedicated, structurally read-only overseer sits above the individual project instances: it reads their state files, event logs, and token logs to produce audit findings, but its own permission file is deny-listed against the write access it's auditing for, so it can never patch what it's checking. It also tracks constitutional drift: diffing today's permissions and exceptions against each project's founding charter, so a series of individually-reasonable exceptions can't quietly erode the original human-in-the-loop guarantees without anyone noticing the cumulative distance.

Two real captures from a live AOS instance (career-os), taken 2026-08-15 — not staged, not a mockup. Names have been switched to first person for this page; everything else is verbatim.

## Human gates (absolute — do not relax without my own explicit go-ahead)
I submit every application, send every message, operate every portal,
and hold every credential myself. Agents draft and score only — no agent
in this system is granted Bash or network-send tools that could submit,
send, or post anything on my behalf.

Logged exception (2026-07-18, my own explicit go-ahead): jd-harvester is
granted Bash, scoped by its own agent-definition text to read-only curl
GET/POST calls against known public, unauthenticated ATS job-listing
JSON APIs only — never for login, submission, message-sending, or any
destination other than these public listing endpoints.

What that gate produces in practice: agents write a scored shortlist to
outbox/ and stop. No agent has the tooling to act on an "80% fit" call by
itself — I read the shortlist and mark a role PURSUE myself before
resume-tailor is allowed to touch it.
  • Filesystem-as-system-bus state: files stand in for the RAM/disk tiers a traditional OS would use, so any agent's work is inspectable and resumable without a database.
  • Tiered model routing: cheap/fast models handle routine dispatch and collection work by default, escalating to a stronger model only for synthesis or architecture-level calls — every completed task logs its model, effort, and token counts, so routing is auditable, not assumed.
  • Human-approval gates: agents draft, score, and shortlist; they don't submit, send, or hold credentials. One narrow, explicitly-logged exception exists (read-only calls to public job listings) — everything else routes through a human decision recorded in the task packet.
  • A structurally read-only usage/governance overseer: audits token and compute usage, permission drift, and cross-project patterns without ever writing back into what it's checking.
  • Task-packet loop, not a chat thread: dispatch queued tasks one at a time, route output through a verifier, pass → done, fail → a two-attempt rule → blocked with a written brief for a human to resolve.
  • Cold-start-safe by design: every orchestrator run assumes zero memory of any prior invocation and resumes purely from a checkpoint file and the task packets on disk, so a scheduled run or a session cut off mid-way picks back up safely.

Daily use

career-os

Multi-agent job-search system · built on AOS

I run my own job search on it, and it cut my application turnaround by roughly 10x.

  • Persistent task-packet queue on disk: a task's folder location is its status, so nothing depends on a chat session's memory.
  • Five named agent roles, each with a narrow job: sourcing, drafting, checking, dispatch, procedure formation.
  • A verifier with no ability to fix anything it finds: no Write/Edit/Bash tools, so it can only report pass or fail with evidence.
  • A two-attempt rule before anything escalates to a written brief for a human decision, instead of retrying forever.
  • Hard human gates on anything externally visible or hard to reverse: no agent submits, sends, or marks a job pursued on its own.
  • Skill formation on genuine repetition only: a manual check gets promoted to a maintained procedure after it's actually repeated, cited by task ID, never speculatively.

I built career-os to run my own job search the way I'd want a program run: nothing moves forward without evidence, and no single agent both does the work and signs off on it. It's a personal tool, not a product. Nine task packets have gone through the pipeline so far across two parallel job-search tracks, and I use it daily. My own estimate is that it's cut my application turnaround by roughly 10x, mostly by removing the manual re-checking I used to do by hand every time.

Proprietary

Brain Vivek

Offline document-intelligence system · directed via Claude Code

This one can't be demoed. Its architecture is fair game to describe; the data never leaves the network.

Illustrative diagram, not a real screenshot — entity labels here are generic placeholders. In practice, entities extracted from a document (a decision, a commitment, a status, a person) become nodes; a question is answered by walking this graph and the local vector index together, then handed to a fully local LLM to phrase the answer — source-cited, with zero data ever leaving the machine.

"A fully offline, air-gap-compliant second brain that ingests 13,000+ documents across email, SharePoint, and OneDrive, extracting entities via spaCy, embedding and indexing them with BGE in SQLite, and linking knowledge through dual NetworkX and Kùzu graphs, orchestrated by a LangGraph agentic pipeline with a local Phi-3-mini LLM. It surfaces grounded, source-cited answers to 'what did we commit, who worked on this, what's the status' in seconds, with zero data leaving the network."

It runs on sensitive material and stays private, but it's the deepest technical evidence of how I actually work with an AI coding agent: I directed Claude Code to design and build every layer of this, from a custom binary-format document parser up through a two-graph knowledge model. Directing that build, and being able to read, debug, and reason about the code it produced, is the actual skill; typing the code myself was never the point.

  • spaCy NER
  • BGE embeddings
  • SQLite (multi-DB)
  • NetworkX + Kùzu graphs
  • LangGraph
  • local Phi-3-mini / Llama fallback
  • pywin32 Outlook COM

Personal app

SnapHabit

Submitted · pending approval

One tap marks today done. That's the whole first screen.

  • Tap-to-complete tracking: mark a habit done for the day in one tap; streaks and stats update immediately.
  • Streak counter with milestones: tracks the current streak per habit and shows progress toward the next one.
  • 90-day heatmap and stats dashboard: a calendar-style heatmap plus completion-rate stats.
  • SnapCoins and badges: in-app coins for completions and streak milestones, with a dedicated achievements screen.
  • Freemium limit: free tier caps tracking at 3 habits; a Pro screen unlocks unlimited habits (UI-level gate today, no live billing wired up yet).
  • Local-first data: everything is stored on-device; no account or server required.
  • Native Android build: React Native/Expo, signed release, tested end-to-end with no crashes.

Most habit trackers bury the one action that actually matters, marking today done, under logins, feeds, and settings screens. SnapHabit is for anyone who wants a fast, low-friction way to build a streak: open the app, tap, done. It's submitted to Google Play and, as of this writing, pending Google's review, not yet publicly live. From here: clear Play Store approval, wire up real in-app billing behind the existing Pro paywall, and bring the same experience to iOS.

Personal app

AppTube

Alpha · closed testing

Pick a name, add a few columns, and it builds you a working tracker. No code.

  • No-code mini apps: pick a name, add up to 6 columns, and it generates a working tracker screen entirely on-device.
  • Ships with a ready-made example: every install starts with a working "Vegetable Order" list, editable and deletable.
  • Save → share → track: a list can be shared as an image and tracked through order states by ticking off what's arrived.
  • History and repeat: past saved lists live in a History tab and can be repeated in one tap.
  • Fully offline: no account, no login, no server round-trip for normal use.
  • Multi-language: English, Hindi, and Marathi, with text sizing tuned for older users.

Not in the alpha

AI-generated mini apps from a text prompt (built, disabled while testing), payments/pricing, and cloud sync: none of these are active in the current build.

A lot of everyday tracking, like a vegetable order list, a simple log, or a small routine, doesn't deserve a full custom app, but generic note-taking apps aren't built for people who find modern app UIs confusing. AppTube lets anyone build a small, purpose-built mini app for a task like this without writing code, aimed first at older, less tech-fluent users. My own parents are the first real testers. It's in alpha testing for its first MVP with a small internal group, not a public launch. Next: broader closed testing, then a wider release once feedback is folded in, with AI-assisted mini-app generation (already built, currently switched off) as a likely next step.

Personal app

Ghar360

Build phase

One on-site video capture becomes a room you can walk through in a browser.

  • Validated end-to-end pipeline: video → COLMAP structure-from-motion → Nerfstudio splatfacto training → PLY export → compression → browser viewer, has produced one working scene from real footage.
  • Live in-browser rendering: renders via three.js with orbit/pan/dolly camera controls, no plugin required.
  • A real web app, not a demo page: a React + Vite frontend with working landing, listing, and tour routes.
  • Repeatable retrain tooling: a COLMAP merge script, a pinned training config with a stated cost estimate, and an atomic compress-and-swap script with revert support.

Known rough edges

  • Only one scene trained so far, with visible reconstruction noise typical of an early splat, not yet a polished "finished tour."
  • Camera bounds still drift slightly at the ceiling and one wall; a fix is scoped, not yet locked in.
  • Nothing is deployed to a public URL yet; this runs from a local dev build.

Buyers routinely commit to visiting or shortlisting properties based on a handful of static photos, which wastes everyone's time and under-sells properties that look better in person. Ghar360 turns one on-site video capture into a walkable, shareable 3D tour a buyer can explore from any browser, aimed at individual builders and small brokerages who can't afford a dedicated 3D-scanning team. It's currently blocked on gathering more source footage to train additional scenes; it's not yet shipped or demoable to a client. Next: a second, higher-quality capture and retrain, then a first real deployment once viewer quality is proven out.
